strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile problem: modelling human response times under changing feedback. Combining task-trained representations, an evidence-accumulation scaffold, and reinforcement learning is a plausible contribution with potential value for cognitive simulation.

The dataset contains 21,157 responses across two days and four feedback conditions, with 36 participants retained for analysis. Repeated measurements and attention/anxiety ratings provide useful experimental context. Links to data and code support reproducibility.

The representation comparison provides evidence that arithmetic-task features improve prediction over the tested raw-number and encoded-number baselines, achieving human-choice accuracy of 0.9613 and response-time MAPE of 0.3652.

Evaluation includes pooled, group-specific, individual-specific, and leave-one-participant-out settings. The hybrid model improves average MAPE over Pure DRL in all four settings, including 0.3037 to 0.2905 under participant holdout, and reports substantially shorter training time.
weaknesses: The central claim of explaining fine-grained human cognitive processes exceeds the evidence. The component called a DDM uses an imposed sigmoid connecting SVM-derived endpoints, without specifying a conventional stochastic diffusion process or validating its cognitive assumptions. Training against final response times cannot uniquely identify intermediate evidence trajectories. Agreement between learned trajectories and aggregate response-time trends therefore does not establish the proposed human mechanism.

The interpretation of learned corrections as time-pressure effects is insufficiently supported. The manuscript does not clearly establish which untreated observations train the purported no-pressure SVM baseline, and Figure 7 shows substantial 'time pressure effect' trajectories even in the no-pressure group. These corrections may absorb baseline prediction errors. Ablations removing visual feedback or replacing frames with a pressure indicator and elapsed time are needed to establish the contribution of dynamic stimulus modelling.

The principal comparison does not isolate the proposed cognitive constraint. Pure DRL simultaneously changes the visual encoder, input dimensionality, action scaling, and episode structure. These differences can affect both accuracy and training speed independently of evidence accumulation. Comparisons with an equally informed supervised response-time regressor, a fitted stimulus-dependent DDM, and controlled trajectory ablations would better establish the advance over existing cognitive/ML combinations.

The predictive gains over Pure DRL are modest: approximately 1.2–4.3% relative MAPE reduction across settings. No confidence intervals, participant-level significance analysis, or variation across training seeds establishes their reliability. The manuscript also needs to specify that every human-supervised stage, including the SVMs, is fitted strictly within each training fold.

The experiments provide limited evidence for the claimed generality under dynamic environments. Participant holdout occurs within the same feedback condition, and displaying predictions chronologically does not establish prospective forecasting. Only one arithmetic task and one repeating progress-bar animation are tested; transfer to new stimulus timings, feedback policies, or cognitive tasks remains un demonstrated.

The behavioural analysis requires clarification. Only 36 of the 50 recruited participants enter the final analysis, including seven in the random-feedback group, and criteria for excluding three 'extreme outlier' participants are unspecified. The description of paired post-hoc tests between independent groups is also unclear. Anxiety has no significant group main effect, so interpreting response-time differences specifically as stress regulation needs stronger support.

Important implementation details are missing, including the precise sigmoid construction, perturbation coefficient lambda, adaptive-feedback thresholds, and treatment of responses beyond the ten-second modelling limit. Minor reporting inconsistencies also warrant correction: Figure 4(a) implies approximately 99.61% arithmetic test accuracy rather than the stated 99.93%, and the termination description confuses the response-time symbol with the evidence threshold. The substantive validation gaps, rather than these minor errors, drive the weak-reject recommendation.
